chunks: "Short answer: avoid it when I can, but I don't treat it as forbidden. A via is a discontinuity: the barrel adds series inductance, roughly a nanohenry for a 1.
6 mm board, the pads and plane cutouts add a few tenths of a picofarad, and whatever barrel is left below the exit layer is a stub that resonates.
Whether that matters depends on the edge rate. A 1 nanohenries via in a 50 ohm line reflects about 1% of a 1 nanoseconds edge, but around 10% of a 100 picoseconds edge.
So on a 20 megahertz SPI line I don't care; on a 10 Gb/s pair I care a lot. When I do have to via, I do four things. One, minimise the count: no layer hopping for convenience.
Two, put a ground via right beside the signal via, so the return current has a short path to the next plane.
Three, keep the stub short, by routing to the layer nearest the exit side, or back-drilling, or using blind or micro vias.
Four, for differential pairs, make both vias identical and symmetric.
And I size the anti-pads so the via impedance is close to the trace, then check the result in a 3D or via-model simulation if the speed justifies it."
